title: Path Stack — Core Method
description: The current search path is a stack: each descent pushes a location, each backtrack pops one, and the top is always where you are. Pushes record not just the location but the decision that led there — which query, which facet — so the path explains itself. The stack has a sane depth cap with the oldest entries summarized rather than dropped, keeping memory bounded on long missions. This simple structure is the backbone of every resumable, explainable navigation session. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Visited Set — Core Method
description: Revisiting locations wastes budget and can loop forever in cyclic archives, so the state manager keeps a visited set with first-visit timestamps. Before any move, the navigator checks the set; revisits are allowed only when explicitly requested, and then they are flagged. Timestamps let old visits expire, so a location explored hours ago can be reconsidered with fresh eyes. The visited set is the memory that turns wandering into systematic exploration. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Session Snapshots — Core Method
description: Long investigations get interrupted, so the state manager serializes the full navigation state — path stack, visited set, frontier, pending decisions — into a snapshot that can be stored and restored later. Snapshots are plain data structures, versioned so old ones still load after the format evolves. Restoring replays the state exactly, and the log of decisions since the snapshot lets the user see what happened in between. Durable sessions turn navigation from a fragile live process into a persistent artifact. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
demo:
import json
state = {"path": ["net", "arch1"], "visited": ["net", "arch1"], "frontier": ["db1"]}
snap = json.dumps(state)
restored = json.loads(snap)
print("snapshot bytes:", len(snap))
print("restored path:", restored["path"])

title: Branch History — Core Method
description: Real exploration branches: you try one path, backtrack, and try another, and the history should remember all of them as a tree, not a single line. The branch history records each decision point with its alternatives and which were tried, so abandoned branches can be resumed instead of rediscovered. Branches are pruned when their frontier is exhausted or their promise drops below threshold. This tree-shaped memory is what separates a research assistant from a goldfish. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
provenance: JAH Databases archive-intelligence tools program, lane T2a — public methods from established computer-science practice.

title: Back-Forward Navigation — Core Method
description: Borrowed from web browsers, the two-stack model gives users back and forward buttons over their own navigation history: moving to a new location pushes the old one onto the back stack and clears forward; going back swaps them. This is intuitive because everyone already understands browser history, and it composes with the path stack underneath. The state manager exposes the same operations to autonomous agents, which use them to retreat from dead ends gracefully. Familiar semantics, machine-usable implementation. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
